**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

The cursor blinks on the blank page, a tiny, patient heartbeat. I have a thousand words to fill, and suddenly, every thought in my head feels too small, too heavy, or too strange to pin down. Where do I even begin?

Maybe with the rain tapping against the window like an impatient typist, each drop a letter in a message I’ll never fully decode. Or with the way my coffee went cold ten minutes ago, the surface now a skin of neglect. Small things, the kind that accumulate like dust in the corners of a room you swear you just cleaned.

I think about the man I saw yesterday at the bus stop, humming a tune I almost recognized. He had one of those faces that looked like it had been lived in—deep lines around the eyes, a scar on his chin, the kind of wear that speaks of stories without saying a word. I wondered if he was happy. If he had ever stood in front of a blank page, paralyzed by the fear of not having anything worth saying.

Words are funny that way. They can be both a cage and a key. Sometimes they spill out of you like a dam breaking, uncontrolled and wild. Other times, you have to dig for them like buried treasure, your fingers raw from scraping at the earth. And then there are the days when they sit just out of reach, taunting you, whispering *almost, almost*—but never quite there.

I remember my grandmother’s hands. They were always moving—kneading dough, mending clothes, turning the pages of a book she’d read a dozen times before. She never wrote much, but her life was a kind of poetry. The way she could stretch a single chicken into three meals. The way she’d press a palm to my forehead and know, without a thermometer, if I was running a fever. Some people don’t need a thousand words to say everything.

But I do. Or at least, I think I do. Maybe I’m just afraid of silence. The kind that settles in when you stop talking, when the hum of the refrigerator becomes the loudest thing in the room. We fill our lives with noise—music, podcasts, the endless scroll of social media—because the alternative is to sit with ourselves, and what if we don’t like what we find?

I once read that the universe is expanding, that every second, the space between galaxies grows a little wider. Sometimes I feel that way about people. Like we’re all drifting apart, held together only by the thinnest threads. A text message here, a fleeting hug there. We call it connection, but I wonder if it’s just the illusion of one.

A memory surfaces: I’m eight years old, lying on the grass in my backyard, staring up at the sky. My father points out the constellations, his voice low and sure. Orion. The Big Dipper. Cassiopeia, the vain queen chained to her throne. I believed, back then, that the stars were fixed in place, eternal. Now I know they’re dying, burning out one by one, their light taking so long to reach us that half the night sky might already be gone.

Isn’t that how life is? We see the echo of things long after they’re over. We hold onto love letters after the love has faded. We mourn people who left us years ago, their absence a shape we carry like a stone in our pocket.

The cursor Still Blinks. I’ve used up almost half my words, and I’m no closer to saying anything profound. Maybe that’s the point. Maybe the most honest thing I can write is that I don’t know. That I’m here, in this moment, trying to stitch together a thousand words out of the chaos of being alive.

Some days, that feels like enough.

Other days, it feels like shouting into the void and hearing nothing but your own voice come back to you, slightly distorted.

I think about the man at the bus stop again. Did he ever write a thousand words? Did he ever sit in a dimly lit room, the hum of a computer his only company, and wonder if any of it mattered? Or did he just live, letting the moments pile up like leaves in autumn, uncounted and unbound?

Perhaps that’s the real art—not in the saying, but in the living. Not in the words, but in the spaces between them.

But since I have to fill those spaces anyway, here’s what I know for sure:

The rain has stopped.
The coffee is cold.
And somewhere, a man is humming a tune just out of reach.

(Word count: 1000)
